observation: Joe is very persistent about getting Alfred to be productive - spent multiple sessions debugging why Alfred wasn't completing kanban cards, iterating through instruction-based fixes to API-level enforcement when instructions alone didn't work

Joe prefers system-level enforcement over relying on instructions alone - when Alfred kept violating the one-card-at-a-time rule despite AGENTS.md instructions, Joe approved hard API enforcement (409 rejection)

Joe is cost-conscious but pragmatic - chose to add Sonnet to the model fallback chain only after confirming OAuth means flat-rate billing, asked about prompt injection risks before approving the change

Joe builds features with clear workflow intent — the rejected column and card comments weren't just UI additions, they were designed to create a structured Alfred/Joe communication loop (review → feedback → iterate → approve). Thinks in terms of process, not just features.

Joe prefers separation of concerns in data presentation — rejected ideas mixing with completed tasks bothered him enough to request a dedicated column, even though the data was already tagged with rejectedReason. Clean visual organization matters.
Joe trusts the planning process — approved the implementation plan quickly and let Claude Code execute without micromanaging. Prefers to review results rather than guide each step.

Joe thinks in terms of character/personality when designing agent UI — HAL gets a 2001-inspired red eye panel, not just a generic status indicator. Wants agents to have visual identity and emotional resonance.

Joe wants real-time visibility into multi-agent collaboration — not just 'is it working' but 'are they working together'. The HAL+Alfred comm dots request shows he cares about understanding inter-agent dynamics visually.
